bull_thesis:
THE BULL CASE FOR RANDSTAD N.V. (RAND.AS) — a probabilistically-weighted argument that this is a cyclical industrial leader at/just past its trough, where the FCF yield pays you to wait for a recovery that has now demonstrably begun.

CORE THESIS: Randstad is the global #1/#2 staffing franchise priced for permanent decline (P/FCF 5.3x, EPS €1.66 vs €5.02 peak) at the precise moment its end-market is inflecting from contraction to growth. The dossier's own green flags confirm the turn is real, not rhetorical: "63% of business in growth" (2026-Q1, up from ~25% at end-2024 and 50% in Q4), a genuine "return to organic revenue growth" of +0.4% after revenue fell every single year 2022→2025 (27.57B→25.43B→24.12B→23.08B), and "manufacturing PMIs back above 50." Staffing is the most operationally-geared early-cycle industry there is — gross profit drops through to EBITA at a high incremental rate once volumes turn because the branch/recruiter cost base is already in place. Management's terminology migration from "adaptability/navigating the cycle" (2024) to "operational gearing" and "scalability" (2026) is the tell: the cost base was cut hard through the trough (€181M lower cost in 2025, "recovery ratio 71%"), so the same revenue line now carries far more profit on the way up than it shed on the way down.

CATALYST 1 — EARNINGS OPERATING LEVERAGE OFF A CRUSHED BASE. The +155.4% YoY EPS jump to €1.66 is real and, crucially, it happened with revenue STILL DOWN -4.3% for the full year. That is the operating-leverage signature: earnings inflecting before revenue. If the +0.4% organic growth of 2026-Q1 sustains and broadens (and 63%-in-growth says the breadth is already there), the same mechanism that took EPS from €0.65 (2024) to €1.66 (2025) on falling revenue compounds violently on RISING revenue. A return toward even half the 2022 peak EPS (€5.02 → ~€2.50) against today's €26.24 price is a sub-11x P/E on a recovering cyclical leader — cheap. The CFO explicitly defended a hard floor: the 3.0% EBITA margin he told Konrad Zomer in 2024-Q2 "should be the lowest" HELD throughout the trough (margins stabilized 3.0–3.3%) — verified delivery on the single most-watched number, and the base from which gearing now works upward.

CATALYST 2 — FREE CASH FLOW IS REAL AND THE BALANCE SHEET IS SELF-HEALING. FCF margin 3.5%, FCF +41.4% YoY, "solid free cash flow of approximately EUR 600 million." At P/FCF 5.3x, the market is handing you a ~19% free-cash-flow yield on a business whose working capital UNWINDS (releases cash) in a downturn and only modestly reverses early in recovery. Net debt of €612M is roughly one year of FCF — eminently serviceable, not distressed. The "strengthening our balance sheet" claim is qualified-honest per the dossier (Section 2: "Match (qualified)"). Even the bearish read on the ~95% payout (€284M dividend on €299M NI) cuts bullish: it signals management confidence that the FCF — not accounting NI — covers the distribution, and the €1.62 dividend on a €26.24 share is a ~6.2% yield you are paid to hold while the option plays out.

CATALYST 3 — A CREDIBLE, MARKET-SHARE-GAINING BRIGHT SPOT. "US Operational grew 8%... double-digit profit growth validates our new model" (2026-Q1) is, per the dossier, "a credible, market-share-gaining bright spot" and the one hard datapoint management offered. In a sector where the US is the bellwether and the highest-margin large market, +8% operational growth with double-digit profit growth is exactly the leading indicator a cyclical bull wants — it shows the specialization model converting to share gains where the cycle has turned first.

CATALYST 4 — THE DIGITAL MARKETPLACE IS A FREE OPTION, CORRECTLY PRICED AT ZERO. The bear's strongest point — that the "€4 billion annualized revenue" marketplace metric flatlined Q3→Q4 and its economics are undisclosed (Verbeek, James Clark/Barclays both stonewalled) — is, for the bull, a feature not a bug at THIS price. At P/FCF 5.3x you are paying nothing for transformation. The institutionalization is concrete: hiring David Koker (ex-Booking.com) as the first "Chief Digital Growth Officer" in 2025-Q4 is real capital and a real org commitment. If the marketplace ever produces a disclosed, growing P&L line, it is pure upside; if it produces nothing, you still own a cyclical leader at a high-teens FCF yield. The director's own framing nails it: "Size to the cyclical thesis, treat the transformation as a free option."

CATALYST 5 — TONE/CONFIDENCE INFLECTION IS CORROBORATED BY THE BREADTH DATA. Unlike the discredited 2024 "green shoots," the 2026-Q1 confidence ("I'm proud of our team's continued execution... current trajectory gives us confidence") is now BACKED by a hard breadth statistic (63% in growth) and PMIs>50 — the macro confirmation the 2024 calls lacked. When Virginia Montorsi asked if anything surprised them, the answer — "nothing major to report" — reads as genuine in-control stability rather than the defensive hedging of 2024.

PROBABILISTIC WEIGHTING & CONDITIONS THAT MUST HOLD: I weight this as roughly a 55–60% probability of a satisfactory-to-strong outcome over a 12–24 month horizon, conditional on three things: (1) the demand inflection is CYCLICAL and durable, not a one-quarter head-fake — the 63%-in-growth breadth and PMIs>50 are the key tells to monitor; (2) gross margin compression (18.7%, -1.10σ below peak) stabilizes as volume returns and mix normalizes — management guided "-80bps then easing through the year" and delivered it, so the trajectory is at least controlled; (3) Eurozone/US industrial activity does not roll back into recession. The asymmetry is the whole point: you are buying a global staffing leader at a ~19% FCF yield and a ~6% dividend yield, where the earnings engine has already proven it inflects before revenue does, the recovery breadth is already visible in the numbers, and the entire "AI transformation" story is yours for free. Even a mediocre operator is mispriced here on the cyclical thesis alone — and Randstad is demonstrably better than mediocre on the metrics that are actually verifiable (cost discipline, FCF, recovery ratio, US share gains).
bear_thesis:
THE BEAR CASE FOR RANDSTAD N.V. (RAND.AS) — a probabilistically-weighted argument that the "transformation" is a cyclical-trough survival story dressed up as strategy, that the stock is NOT cheap on the screener's own math, and that the structural AI threat to the staffing TAM is precisely the risk management is pre-emptively defending.

CORE THESIS — IT IS NOT CHEAP, FULL STOP. The bull case leans on "valuation cushion," but the screener's own authoritative output contradicts the dossier's marketing of "61% margin of safety." The metrics_str is explicit: Price 26.24 vs Fair Value 19.94 → Margin of Safety -18%. The stock trades roughly 18% ABOVE the model's fair value. The dossier's repeated "61% margin of safety / P/FCF 5.6x" claim is internally inconsistent with the screener and should be treated as a red flag about the narrative, not a green flag about the price. A "cheap" multiple on a cyclical at a cyclical INFLECTION is the classic value trap: you are paying ~6x peak-ish-recovery FCF for a business whose 3-yr revenue CAGR is -5.8%, whose 5-yr EPS CAGR is -20.2%, and whose net margin is a razor-thin 1.3%. P/FCF 5.3x on FCF that is itself flattered by trough working-capital release is not a margin of safety — it is the bait.

RISK 1 — THE GROWTH IS A SINGLE QUARTER AGAINST A MULTI-YEAR CONTRACTION, AND MANAGEMENT HAS BEEN WRONG ABOUT EXACTLY THIS BEFORE. The bull's headline catalyst — "return to organic revenue growth" of +0.4% — is dismantled in the dossier's own forensic table: "Diverges. A single +0.4% quarter against a multi-year contraction. Story is richer than trajectory justifies." Revenue fell EVERY year 2022→2025 (27.57B→23.08B). More damning: this same management team called "green shoots" and "bottoming out" in 2024-Q1 and 2024-Q2 and "they were wrong for over a year" — revenue kept declining through 2025-Q2. Konrad Zomer explicitly challenged the gap and predicted "Q2 could be quite a weak quarter, not just transitional" — HE WAS RIGHT. The guidance-credibility section is unambiguous: 43% earnings-beat rate (3 of 7 quarters) — BELOW A COIN FLIP. When a team with a sub-50% beat rate and a documented year-long recovery-timing miss tells you the cycle has turned, the base rate says discount it heavily. The +155% YoY EPS "recovery" is the same trick: "flatters off a catastrophic 2024 base (€0.65)"; absolute EPS €1.66 "remains a third of the 2022 peak."

RISK 2 — THE ENTIRE TRANSFORMATION THESIS RESTS ON A METRIC MANAGEMENT REFUSES TO QUANTIFY. This is "the biggest non-answer in the dossier." The "€4 billion annualized revenue" digital marketplace was "repeated verbatim in Q4 with zero progress" — Maarten Verbeek caught it not moving Q3→Q4 and got "a matter of technicalities." James Clark (Barclays, 2026-Q1) asked directly for the marketplace profit contribution and Van't Noordende deflected: "it's hard to tell at this particular point in time... a work in progress." A transformation worth a re-rating that cannot produce a single disclosed, growing P&L line after multiple quarters of direct analyst pressure is, on the balance of evidence, not producing economics. The "AI optimist" monologue in 2026-Q1 ("6-7% job loss... where our exposure is limited") is, per Hidden Signals, "defensive armor, not offense" — "management is managing the bear case before being asked." That is what a team does when it fears the question is existential: AI structurally shrinking the staffing TAM is the terminal risk, and the lengthy unprompted defense is the tell that management itself is worried.

RISK 3 — THE "GROWTH" ACTIVELY DILUTES PROFITABILITY (STRUCTURAL, NOT CYCLICAL, MARGIN EROSION). Gross margin is 18.7% and CONTRACTING, sitting -1.10σ below its historical peak. Under repeated pressure from Simon LeChipre (Jefferies), management conceded the honest sub-text: growth is "concentrated in lower-margin large clients and lower-margin geographies." So the very revenue inflection the bull celebrates comes at a structurally worse mix — the more they grow, the more gross margin dilutes. This breaks the operating-leverage thesis: if incremental revenue carries below-average gross margin AND the cost base must re-inflate as volumes return (recruiters, branches, idle-time reversing), the "scalability/operating gearing" story underdelivers. Net margin of 1.3% leaves essentially no cushion for the gross-margin mix drag.

RISK 4 — CAPITAL ALLOCATION IS DEFENSIVE-TO-IMPRUDENT, AND INSIDERS WON'T BUY. Two flags compound. First, ~95% dividend payout: €284M dividend on €299M net income while carrying €612M net debt and contracting margins — "distributing nearly all earnings rather than deleveraging or reinvesting through the trough." If the recovery stalls, management has signaled it will prioritize the dividend over the balance sheet, which is exactly backward for a leveraged cyclical. Second, and decisive: Insider buy ratio 0.00 — "no management conviction expressed through their own capital." The people closest to the marketplace economics, the mix problem, and the durability of +0.4% are NOT buying the stock at €26.24. When the narrative is "couldn't be better positioned for a more complete recovery" but insiders put up zero of their own money, weight the wallets over the words.

RISK 5 — THE TRACK RECORD OF FAILED BETS AND REDUCED TRANSPARENCY. The Monster/CareerBuilder merger, touted in 2024-Q2 for "significant scale benefits," was quietly deconsolidated by September 2024 and now survives only as a margin footnote — a failed capital-allocation move. Torc (the marketplace acquisition hyped in 2024-Q2) "has vanished from the narrative entirely." This is the SAME management team now asking for credit on a new digital story. Simultaneously, in 2026-Q1 they "removed the regional subsegments in Europe" — reducing disclosure granularity in a period of mixed regional performance, a transparency reduction precisely when scrutiny of where the growth is (and isn't) matters most.

UNQUANTIFIED WILDCARD — NETHERLANDS LEGISLATION ON THE #1 MARKET. Zomer (2025-Q4) pressed on +15% bill-rate inflation from pension/CLA changes hurting volumes in Randstad's largest market; management dismissed the figure as "way too high" and called the impact "too early to tell" — left unquantified. A volume hit on the home market would directly undercut the breadth statistic the bull relies on.

PROBABILISTIC WEIGHTING & WHAT WOULD CONFIRM THE BEAR. I weight a disappointing outcome (flat-to-negative total return, or a re-rating DOWN toward the €19.94 fair value, i.e. ~24% downside) at roughly 40–45% over 12–24 months — materially higher than a "cheap cyclical" framing implies, because the stock is above model fair value, the inflection is one quarter from a team with a 43% beat rate, and the transformation premium rests on undisclosed economics. The bear is CONFIRMED if any of the following print: (1) the +0.4% organic growth fails to broaden or reverses in 2026-Q2/Q3 — the precise 2024 "green shoots" failure mode; (2) gross margin keeps compressing below 18.7% as large-client/low-margin-geography mix worsens, proving the growth is dilutive; (3) the marketplace remains unquantified for another quarter or two (the €4B figure stays frozen), confirming there are no economics to disclose; (4) management cuts or strains the dividend, revealing the €612M net debt was the binding constraint all along; (5) AI-driven structural pressure shows up as a falling permanent-placement/operational TAM that the cyclical recovery cannot offset. The asymmetry the bull ignores: you are NOT being paid a fat discount to fair value (you are paying a -18% premium to it), the earnings "recovery" is arithmetic off a €0.65 base, and the strategic re-rating story is asserted, never evidenced, by a team that already failed publicly at Monster/CareerBuilder and will not put its own capital into the shares.

# Randstad N.V. (RAND.AS) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator: Claude Opus 4.8 · Investment-committee forensic review · Source: 6 consecutive earnings calls Q1-2024 → Q1-2026 (FMP transcripts) cross-referenced against the screener financial trajectory FY2021–FY2025 + TTM to 2026-03-31.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Randstad management has told across these six calls is remarkably **stationary** — it is the same narrative repeated for two-and-a-half years, with the only real evolution being *which quarter* the promised recovery is supposed to arrive.

- **Q1-2024 (Apr-2024):** "Green shoots… things appear to be bottoming out." CEO van't Noordende frames Q2 as "somewhat of a transition quarter… hopefully into a more pronounced recovery." Revenue −7.8% YoY, gross margin 20.2%, EBITA margin 3.0%, recovery ratio 46%. The dominant theme is the *Partner for Talent* strategy: four specializations (Operational, Professional, Digital, Enterprise), the digital marketplace rollout, and the Randstad Talent platform.
- **Q2-2024 (Jul-2024):** The green shoots wilt — "not all green shoots that we saw at the end of Q1 have grown as well as we would have liked." Revenue −7.5%, gross margin 19.8%, EBITA 3.0%. Management explicitly concedes it is **"willing to sacrifice short-term profitability for midterm recovery potential"** and calls 3.0% "the lowest" margin of the year. First mention of M&A appetite ("a few in the pipeline") and the Monster/CareerBuilder merger.
- **Q1-2025 (Apr-2025):** "Solid start." Revenue −4.2% (decline rate moderating). Tariff/geopolitical uncertainty enters the script ("macroeconomic uncertainty has gone up, which is limiting visibility"). The pitch shifts toward **margin protection** — "approximately €60 million savings year-over-year," scenario planning for a tariff-driven US recession. Capital Markets Day held the next day.
- **Q4/FY-2025 (Feb-2026):** The transformation-win lap. FY revenue €23.1B (−2%), EBITA €720M (3.1% margin), recovery ratio **71%**, FCF ~€600M, €181M lower cost YoY. "Over 50% of the business in growth vs ~25% at end-2024." Dividend €1.62 proposed. New Chief Digital Growth Officer (ex-Booking.com). Exit rate "solid," January "flattish."
- **Q1-2026 (Apr-2026):** The first quarter of *reported* organic growth — "63% of Randstad now in growth… 0.4% growth for the quarter." But revenue still €5.5B and **EBITA margin slipped to 2.7%** (from 3.0% in Q1-2025). A long, defensive set-piece on AI ("we are AI optimist… the great adaptation of the workforce") signals the new investor anxiety management must now pre-empt.

**Arc verdict:** The growth drivers introduced early (specialization, digital marketplace, Torc) are still present and have *not* been quietly dropped — but neither have they produced the inflection promised since Q1-2024. The narrative has migrated from "recovery is imminent" (2024) → "we are protecting profitability while we wait" (2025) → "we are technically in growth, and by the way AI is a tailwind not a threat" (2026). The recovery has been perpetually one-to-two quarters away for ten consecutive quarters.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Things appear to be bottoming out… green shoots" | Q1-2024 | Revenue went on to fall every quarter through FY2025; FY24 rev €24.1B → FY25 €23.1B | **Premature by ~2 years.** Bottoming claim recycled across 6 calls. |
| "3.0% EBITA… this should be the lowest" | Q2-2024 | Q1-2026 EBITA margin came in *below* at **2.7%**; net margin 1.3% FY25 | **Missed.** The asserted floor was broken. |
| "Recovery ratio very strong at 71% for the year" | FY-2025 | Corroborated — cost-out of €181M YoY is real and drove the EPS rebound | **TRUE.** This is the genuine achievement. |
| EPS "+155.4% YoY" rebound | FY-2025 | Real but off a collapsed base: EPS €0.65 (FY24) → €1.66 (FY25); still far below €5.02 (FY22). 5-yr EPS CAGR **−20.2%** | **Technically true, misleading framing.** A bounce within a multi-year halving. |
| "Solid free cash flow of approximately €600M" | FY-2025 | TTM FCF €622M corroborates; P/FCF 5.6x. FCF is the load-bearing fact of the value case | **TRUE.** Cash generation is intact. |
| "63% of Randstad now in growth… 0.4% growth" | Q1-2026 | Q1-2026 reported revenue −2.5% YoY in absolute EUR (FX/scope); EPS €0.35 vs €0.44, NI −20% | **Half-true.** "In growth" is an organic, mix-weighted, ex-perm framing; the actual P&L still shrank and margin fell. |

**Synthesis:** Where the claim is about *cash and cost discipline* (FCF ~€600M, €181M cost-out, 71% recovery ratio), the numbers fully corroborate — this is a well-run, cash-generative operator. Where the claim is about *the top-line cycle turning* (green shoots, bottoming, growth), the narrative has been consistently richer than the trajectory justified, for ten quarters. The EPS "+155%" headline is the single most flattering framing in the file and must be read against the −20% 5-yr EPS CAGR and a halving of net income from the 2022 peak.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: STABLE-to-modestly-Rising on tone, but the confidence has migrated from top-line conviction to cost-control conviction.**

- **Q1-2024 — cautiously offensive:** "If the recovery comes, it can come fast… as far as I'm concerned, it comes at the highest possible speed." Hope-led.
- **Q2-2024 — defensive pivot:** "No one in the organization is happy… seeing a 3.0% EBITA margin." Candid, somewhat deflated; "willing to sacrifice profitability."
- **Q1-2025 — guarded/macro-hedged:** "Macroeconomic uncertainty has gone up, which is limiting visibility… too early to say with any certainty." Heavy tariff caveats.
- **FY-2025 — confident on execution, hedged on macro:** "We couldn't be better positioned for a more complete recovery." Confidence is now explicitly about *transformation*, not the market.
- **Q1-2026 — measured, faintly upbeat:** "Volume trends in early April have been encouraging… manufacturing PMIs above 50 in most of our markets for the first time in many, many quarters." Notably calm on geopolitics ("very limited impact").

The language shifted decisively from **offensive (growth/investment)** in early 2024 to **defensive (efficiency/cost/adaptability/recovery-ratio)** through 2025, and is only now tentatively re-acquiring an offensive register ("operational gearing," "scalability") — but always as a *forward* promise, never a delivered result. - **Beat rate:** the screener records 3/7 quarters beating (43%) — a sub-coin-flip hit rate that corroborates the "MEDIUM, leans optimistic on macro" read. No evidence of deliberate sandbagging; if anything the bias is mild over-optimism on the demand turn.

**Score: Medium.** Trust the cost/cash guidance; discount the recovery-timing guidance.

- **The margin floor (Konrad Zomer, ABN AMRO, Q2-2024 and recurrently):** analysts repeatedly probe whether 3.0% EBITA is the trough and whether further profitability will be sacrificed. Management's "this should be the lowest" was subsequently broken — a question that turned into bad news.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these eight quarters is the slow, disciplined management of a **late-cycle staffing trough** — and the gradual replacement of a "we're navigating a downturn" narrative with a "we're emerging transformed" narrative. The arc has three distinct acts.

**Act I — "Stabilization / bottoming" (Q2 2024 – Q1 2025).** The opening frame is unambiguously defensive. Q2 2024: "trading conditions remained challenging across many of our markets," revenue −7.5% YoY, EBITA margin 3.0%, "the last four quarter recovery ratio of 44%." Management leans hard on the language of *adaptability*, *field steering*, *recovery ratio*, and *indirect cost reduction* — the vocabulary of a company defending profitability into a falling top line. The recurring tell is "green shoots that we saw... have not grown as well as we would have liked" (Q2 2024). North America, France, Netherlands, Germany are repeatedly named as the laggards; Spain, Italy, Belgium, Japan as the bright spots. The CEO openly concedes "no one in the organization is happy... seeing a 3.0% EBITA margin" (Q2 2024, Vazquez).

**Act II — "Transformation underway" (Q2 2025 – Q4 2025).** The narrative pivots from cyclical defense to **structural self-improvement**. The load-bearing new theme is the *"partner for talent" strategy* — specialization "at scale is now a fact" (Q2 2025), the *digital marketplace* (rolled to 9 markets, ~€4B annualized run-rate by Q4 2025, "1.4 million shifts self-scheduled... up 30% q/q"), and a *"digital-first"* identity reinforced by hiring a Chief Digital Growth Officer from Booking.com (Q4 2025). Crucially, by Q4 2025 management can point to a hard internal metric of recovery: **"over 50% of the business in growth compared to around 25% at the end of 2024,"** and a **"recovery ratio... very strong at 71% for the year."** The Monster/CareerBuilder job-board has been quietly deconsolidated (a drag removed, ~€60M of gross profit out, mentioned only when an analyst probes the margin bridge).

**Act III — "Return to growth" (Q1 2026).** The most offensive call of the set. "63% of Randstad now in growth, up from 50% in Q4, which equates to 0.4% growth for the quarter" — the first organic-growth print in roughly three years. US operational +8%, manufacturing PMIs "above 50 in most of our markets for the first time in many, many quarters." **Drivers introduced:** digital marketplace / Torc, specialization framework, Zorgwerk (Dutch healthcare acquisition), the 10x10x10 commercial initiative (Q1 2026). **Drivers quietly dropped or de-emphasized:** Monster/CareerBuilder (merged then deconsolidated, now silent); the early "pending recovery" timing promises of 2024 (recovery arrived ~18 months later than the 2024 "green shoots" framing implied).

bull_thesis:
The case for owning Randstad is that the world's largest staffing company is nine months into a genuine cyclical turn and the market is still valuing it on trough earnings. After eleven consecutive quarters of shrinking revenue, growth returned in the first quarter of 2026 (+0.4% organic) and broadened in the second (+1.9%, against a consensus of about 1.0%). The breadth is the point: the share of the business actually growing went from about 25% at the end of 2024, to over 50% by the fourth quarter of 2025, to 63% by the first quarter of 2026. Germany, the market investors watch most closely, swung from -4% to +4% in a single quarter; the United Kingdom and France crossed back into growth; and United States operational staffing has now grown for six straight quarters, up 13% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. Manufacturing purchasing-manager surveys are above 50 in most of Randstad's markets for the first time in years, which is the classic leading indicator for temporary-staffing volume.

Onto that recovering volume, management has bolted a permanently cheaper cost base. Operating costs in 2025 were EUR 181 million below 2024, headcount has been reduced for eight consecutive quarters, and the digital marketplace and central talent centres have lifted the number of workers each Randstad employee can service by 6% to 7% year over year. The company captured the second quarter's seasonal demand, in the chief financial officer's words, "without adding any new capacity." If revenue returns toward the mid-EUR-20-billion range while the cost base stays where it is, the operating margin before amortization can travel from 3.1% back toward the 4% to 4.5% this company earned in 2021 and 2022. Because gross profit is a thin slice of revenue, that swing is enormous in earnings terms: mid-cycle earnings of roughly EUR 3.20 to EUR 3.90 per share against the EUR 1.78 earned over the last twelve months is the entire bull case in one number.

Management has also earned the benefit of the doubt. Across the five calls reviewed, cost commitments were over-delivered (EUR 181 million against roughly EUR 60 million promised entering 2025), the German bottoming call was correct, the Dutch labour-legislation call was correct, and management publicly corrected an analyst who had over-estimated Dutch bill-rate inflation, saying "that's way, way too high" - and was right. The balance sheet supports the wait: leverage is 1.8 times, net debt fell EUR 66 million year over year, and shareholders are paid EUR 1.62 a year, about 4.4% at the current price, while the cycle does its work. Portfolio discipline is improving too, with the subscale technology and consulting units in Australia, France, Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg being sold to LTM for EUR 160 million, removing roughly EUR 469 million of low-margin revenue.

What must hold for this to work: gross margin has to stop falling. The bull case requires the current compression to be cyclical mix - depressed permanent placement and professional staffing, which recover late in every cycle - so that as those high-fee businesses return, the spread and the volume rise together. It also requires the European industrial recovery to survive oil near USD 89 a barrel and a tariff regime that is being rebuilt.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not dispute that volumes have turned. It disputes that the turn is worth anything to a shareholder buying at EUR 37.

Randstad earns a spread: it bills a worker's hours to a client and keeps the difference. That spread has compressed for four consecutive years - gross margin of 20.86% in 2022, 20.76% in 2023, 19.49% in 2024, 18.67% in 2025, and 18.2% in the second quarter of 2026 against 18.9% a year earlier. The consequence is the single most important number in this file: in the celebrated second quarter of 2026, gross profit - the fee the company actually keeps - fell roughly 2% year over year even as revenue grew 1.9%. Every euro of that quarter's profit improvement came from cutting costs, not from earning more. That is cost gearing on a shrinking fee base, and it has a floor: costs are already EUR 181 million below 2024 and headcount has been cut for eight quarters running.

There is good reason to think the compression is structural rather than cyclical. Management has told us repeatedly who the new customer is. Growth is "largely led by increasing demand in large clients" (second quarter of 2026), and a year earlier the chief financial officer conceded the mechanism outright: large clients "are growing high single digits. That has an impact in our margin. It's the market as it is today." Randstad is winning share by being the fastest and cheapest supplier into professional procurement departments, which is precisely the customer set least willing to leave a spread on the table. Worse, the company is automating its own fee away and presenting it as an achievement: the Torc platform delivers "50% lower recruiting cost and 50% shorter time to fill." In a competitive market, that saving ends up in the client's pocket.

The high-spread third of the business - professional, permanent placement, digital and recruitment-process outsourcing - has been shrinking for three years and was still down 6% and 3% respectively in the latest quarter. When the chief executive volunteered an unprompted defence against artificial intelligence in the first quarter of 2026, he defended the operational and health-care two-thirds as "human-centric and minimally impacted by AI." By omission, he conceded the rest. An analyst asked the structural-versus-cyclical question directly in the second quarter of 2025 and was told it was purely cyclical; four quarters later, professional is still declining.

The reported profit is also softer than it looks. The EUR 182 million everyone quotes for the second quarter is an adjusted figure; statutory operating profit was EUR 145 million and net income EUR 84 million. For the 2025 full year the same gap runs EUR 720 million adjusted against EUR 512 million statutory. Roughly EUR 200 million a year of amortization and "one-off" costs is excluded, and those items have recurred in every year of this sequence. Return on invested capital is about 6% and return on equity 8.2%, both below any plausible cost of capital. Cash conversion is deteriorating exactly as growth arrives: free cash flow in the second quarter of 2026 was EUR 39 million against EUR 82 million a year earlier, and the chief financial officer conceded that growth "does require investments in working capital" without quantifying it.

Finally, the price. The shares are up about 74% from the 52-week low of EUR 21.30 and sit roughly 29% above the 200-day average of EUR 28.70. At EUR 37.05 they trade at about 21 times trailing earnings, 19 times the 2026 consensus of EUR 1.94, and 9.8 times enterprise value to reported cash profits - a premium to Adecco at 9.6 times and ManpowerGroup at 8.6 times on live prices - and above the sixteen-analyst consensus target of EUR 34.14 that was itself raised 9.5% on 25 July, after the results. The market is no longer pricing terminal decline. It is pricing a full cyclical recovery that has not yet reached the fee line.
consensus_delta:
For a deep-value candidate the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable or growing earning power. Five weeks ago the answer was clearly yes. Today it is no, and that is the central finding.

At the EUR 21.30 low the market was pricing structural obsolescence into a solvent, cash-generative, number-one global franchise. That was a genuine mispricing, and it has been corrected - by somebody else. Consensus has flipped from disbelief to endorsement: sixteen analysts carry a EUR 34.14 target that was raised 9.5% on 25 July, the sell side upgraded across the sector, and the hiring recovery is now the headline on every desk. The shares trade about 8.5% above that freshly-raised target.

Where we still disagree with the market is narrower, and it points the other way. The street is extrapolating a volume recovery into an earnings recovery, and the fee line does not yet support it. forcing_function:
For a deep-value candidate the forcing function is the event that makes the market re-rate the earning power. The honest answer is that the one available forcing function has already fired, and no dated replacement exists.

What fired: the second-quarter results on 22 July 2026, which converted the cyclical turn from a management claim into a reported number and moved the shares as much as 11.58% in a session. Ahead of it, ManpowerGroup's mid-July beat had already triggered the sector read-across. Consensus targets were then raised 9.5% to EUR 34.14 on 25 July. That sequence is the re-rating, and it is complete.

What remains is calendar rather than catalyst. Third-quarter results are the next scheduled print and are at least as likely to test the thesis as confirm it, given management's own guidance for a subdued July and August and a further gross-margin decline. The 2026 full-year results in February 2027 carry the dividend decision, and a step up in the distribution or a first share repurchase under the capital-allocation policy would be a genuine if modest re-rating event; there is no repurchase authorization in place today. There is no activist, no strategic process, no governance reset and no break-up premise. The sum-of-the-parts discount that would attract an activist does not exist on the numbers - the one arm's-length transaction management has actually struck cleared at roughly the group multiple, which is the strongest available evidence against a hidden parts discount. valley_of_death:
There is no solvency event here. Leverage is 1.8 times, net debt fell EUR 66 million year over year, and there is no visible maturity wall. The risk over the next three to nine months is to the cash flow and to the share price, not to the balance sheet.

The cash-flow hump is already visible and is a direct consequence of the recovery itself. Staffing firms fund their clients' payrolls, so growth consumes working capital before it produces cash. Free cash flow in the second quarter of 2026 was EUR 39 million against EUR 82 million a year earlier, more than halved, on higher working capital and tax. Days of sales outstanding sit at about 89, stretched by the shift toward large clients. Asked directly to size the drag, the chief financial officer conceded the mechanism - growth "does require investments in working capital" - then redirected to full-year framing and declined to quantify it. Critically, the 2025 free cash flow of about EUR 600 million that anchors the cheap cash-flow multiple was flattered by a working-capital release management itself described as a "spillover effect from the very strong 2025." The tax line compounds it: guidance is 28% to 30%, on the full implementation of the global minimum-tax rules, an unfavourable jurisdictional mix, and the temporary French corporate income-tax surcharge.

The macro window is the larger risk, and it is unusually two-sided right now. The whole thesis rests on manufacturing surveys staying above 50 and on the German and French industrial recovery holding. Brent crude is near USD 89 with the Strait of Hormuz blockade reinstated since mid-July, which is a direct tax on exactly the European industrial demand that drives Randstad's operational business. The United States tariff architecture is being rebuilt: the emergency tariff authority sunset on 24 July and the proposed replacement, covering 60 economies at 10% to 12.5%, is not yet final and carries retaliation risk the prior universal regime did not. And the policy-rate backdrop is hostile to a cyclical re-rating, with a December rate rise the priced base case at roughly two-in-three - so this thesis gets no help from falling rates, and must not be underwritten as though it will.

The specific near-term event that hurts is third-quarter results. Management has already conceded that July and August are seasonally subdued with the growth concentrated in September, and has guided gross margin down again. A quarter showing continued volume growth alongside another 30 to 50 basis points of margin decline and weak cash conversion would strip the operating-leverage framing out of a share price that has already paid for it.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to harvest here, and a prospective buyer should understand that the mechanical flow has recently run in the opposite direction.

This is not a dividend-cut or strategic-pivot story. The EUR 1.62 dividend was declared with the 2025 results in line with a stated capital-allocation policy management has consistently honoured, went ex on 31 March 2026 and was paid on 8 April 2026. Nothing threatens the income-focused holder, so there is no yield-driven liquidation to buy into.

The relevant positioning fact is the reverse one. Over the last five weeks the shares absorbed a wave of buying: a sector-wide re-rating in which every major staffing name rose 57% to 110% from its lows, sell-side upgrades across the group, and a value-and-recovery crowd rotating into European cyclicals. Meanwhile the screener's own positioning fields still show a low smart-money score of 14 out of 100 and neutral institutional flow, and insider buying is zero - no member of management bought a share through the entire decline to EUR 21.30 or the recovery from it. So the buying that lifted the shares 74% was not informed insider accumulation or patient institutional building; it was fast money chasing a cycle turn.

That matters for the shape of the risk. Positioning across the wider market is full, with the July fund-manager survey showing cash at 3.6%, a formal contrarian sell signal, and in that condition negative surprises travel considerably farther than positive ones. A crowded, recently-doubled cyclical with no natural holder base and no insider support is exactly the profile that gaps down on a soft print. The forced-selling opportunity worth waiting for has not happened here; the melt-up has.
moderator_conclusion:
Randstad is a good business having a real recovery at a price that has already paid for it. The right action is to wait for the wash-out rather than to buy here.

Three findings drive the call, and none of them is that the catalyst is spent - a fired event is neither a plus nor a penalty in this book, and what has been judged is the residual value case.

First, the recovery is a volume recovery, not yet an earnings recovery. In the second quarter of 2026 revenue grew 1.9% and the shares rose as much as 11.58%, but gross profit - the fee Randstad actually keeps after paying the worker - fell about 2% year over year, because gross margin slipped to 18.2% from 18.9%. Every euro of the quarter's profit improvement came from cost reduction, a lever that is eight quarters old and finite. This is the fourth consecutive year of spread compression, down from 20.86% in 2022, and management guided it lower again on all five calls reviewed. Until gross profit grows faster than revenue, the operating leverage this price assumes remains unproven.

Second, the valuation has closed. At EUR 37.05 the shares sit about 3% above the reconciled base-case value of EUR 36 - a figure two independent methods agree on, a parts-based valuation on enterprise value to gross profit and a normalized-earnings cross-check at 13 times about EUR 2.80. They trade at 9.8 times enterprise value to cash profits against Adecco's 9.6 and ManpowerGroup's 8.6, so this is a premium to peers rather than a discount; the supplied cheap-versus-peers note was computed before the sector re-rated and on a flattered cash-flow figure. And they trade about 8.5% above the sixteen-analyst consensus target of EUR 34.14 that was itself raised on 25 July, after the results. A deep-value candidate whose price exceeds both the analyst consensus and our own fair value has stopped being a deep-value candidate.

Third, the moat is eroding, and that caps what the value case can be worth. The scale and route-density advantage is real, and the digital marketplace genuinely lifts fill rates and raises workers serviced per employee by 6% to 7% a year. But none of it is being retained: gross margin down four straight years, operating margin before amortization down from about 4.4% at the 2022 peak to 3.1%, return on invested capital of roughly 6% and return on equity of 8.2%, all below any plausible cost of capital. Randstad is winning share by being the cheapest and fastest supplier to large procurement departments, and it is halving the cost of its own service - the Torc platform delivers "50% lower recruiting cost" - in a market competitive enough that the saving goes to the client. That is a structural deflation of labour-arbitrage economics. It is material for the high-fee professional third of the business, though not terminal for the operational and health-care two-thirds, which remain genuinely defensible against automation this decade.

The regime backdrop reinforces the timing rather than driving the call. This thesis depends on a single shared macro driver, the global industrial and labour cycle, and so does every one of its peers - which is why all five moved 57% to 110% off their lows together. That is sector beta on one unresolved question, not name-specific edge, and it should not be sized as though it were. It also sits badly against oil near USD 89 with the Hormuz blockade reinstated, a proposed replacement tariff regime that lands on European exporters, and a December rate rise as the priced base case, which means no help from falling rates. Positioning is full, and in this tape negative surprises travel farther than positive ones.

What would change the call. The business deserves to stay on the list: management is credible and has delivered what it promised, the balance sheet is sound at 1.8 times leverage, shareholders are paid about 4.4%, and the operating direction is genuinely improving. The level to wait for is roughly EUR 29 to EUR 30 - back toward the 200-day average of EUR 28.70 - where the parts-based work implies a real double-digit discount instead of a small premium and the free-cash-flow yield becomes compelling again. The alternative route in, without waiting for that price, is to require the proof: two or three consecutive quarters in which gross profit grows faster than revenue, converting the volume story into an earnings story. Neither condition is met today, so the position is a watch, not a buy.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story travels a clean arc from *survival* to *vindication* — and management deserves credit for how little the story wobbled on the way.

**Early 2025 — protect the floor.** The opening posture was defensive and honest about it. Chief executive Sander van 't Noordende opened Q1 2025 with "we were able to protect our bottom line," and the operative verbs were protect, adapt, steer. The chief financial officer, Jorge Vazquez, framed the entire quarter as cost discipline: "our gross profit and OpEx were aligned allowing us to protect relative profitability despite the lower top line." Revenue was falling 4.2% and the honest admission was that visibility had gone: "macroeconomic uncertainty has gone up, which is limiting visibility."

**Mid 2025 — the new normal.** By Q2 2025 uncertainty had been reframed from a shock into a permanent condition — "which, frankly, we and many of our clients see as the new normal." The emphasis shifted from cost defence toward the strategic build: specialization, digital marketplaces, the "partner for talent" programme. This is where the *transformation* narrative started carrying weight the financials could not yet carry.

**Early 2026 — the turn is claimed.** The Q4 2025 call (February 2026) is the hinge. Management produced its first genuinely forward-leaning claim in two years: "we now have over 50% of the business in growth compared to around 25% at the end of 2024," a December exit rate described as solid, and a January trend described as flattish. A new chief digital growth officer was hired from Booking.com — a signal about where the story was heading.

**Mid 2026 — vindication, and a pre-emptive defence.** Q1 2026 delivered the return to organic growth (+0.4%, with 63% of the business growing), and Q2 2026 broadened it (+1.9%, with Germany and the United Kingdom back to growth). But the most revealing passage of the whole sequence is unprompted: in Q1 2026 the chief executive volunteered a long, structured defence of the business against artificial intelligence — citing studies pointing to "a job loss of 6% to 7% over the next 5 to 10 years," and arguing that "Randstad operational and health care are 2/3 of our business today. These are typically jobs that are human-centric and minimally impacted by AI." Management does not spend four minutes of prepared remarks pre-empting a question unless it knows that question is the one holding the shares down.

**Quietly dropped:** the digital marketplace revenue milestone. It was introduced with fanfare (about €4 billion annualized), then stalled — an analyst caught it in February 2026: "In the third quarter, you mentioned that your digital marketplace generated EUR 4 billion in annualized revenue, and exactly the same you mentioned today. So why haven't we seen any progress quarter-on-quarter?" The metric has since been replaced in the script by shift counts, which grow faster and mean less.

A cost that recurs annually is not a one-off, and a multiple built on the adjusted number overstates what the business earns by close to 30%.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — genuinely, and earned.** This is the strongest dimension in the file.

- **Q1 2025 — defensive, hedged.** "It's too early to say with any certainty what impact this will have on our markets and on our future performance." On protecting margin: "It's impossible to guarantee, but that's how we're looking at the year."
- **Q2 2025 — steady, strategy-forward.** "All in all, we're absolutely on the right track." The confidence is about the plan, not the numbers.
- **Q4 2025 — the first forward commitment.** "We couldn't be better positioned for a more complete recovery." And on 2026: "I'm pretty sure we've built the ability to improve the results and profitability going forward" — the first unhedged forward statement in the sequence.
- **Q1 2026 — confident, and confident enough to take on the bear case.** "The current trajectory of our business gives us confidence for the months ahead," plus the unprompted artificial-intelligence defence.
- **Q2 2026 — assured.** "This gives me confidence in our ability to show progress for the rest of the year in both revenue and profit growth."

The language migrated from defensive (protect, adapt, steer, adaptability) to offensive (capture, gearing, scalability, accelerate). Importantly, the specificity moved in the same direction: by Q1 2026 the chief financial officer was giving quarter-ahead gross-margin bridges to ten basis points. Executives who are worried get vaguer, not more precise. This one got more precise.

The one asymmetry worth flagging: confidence rose fastest on *revenue* and stayed carefully hedged on *margin*. Every single call in this sequence guided gross margin down. That is not a company that believes its spread is about to recover.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is a management team that says what will happen and is then largely right — including when the news is bad.

Tracked promises against later delivery:

- **Cost.** Q1 2025 promised roughly €60m of year-over-year savings entering the year with "headroom into the next quarters." The 2025 outturn was €181m lower costs and a 71% recovery ratio. **Over-delivered.**
- **Gross margin.** Q2 2025 guided a Q3 seasonal dip of "around 20 to 30 basis points" plus a foreign-exchange drag. Q1 2026 guided the Q2 temp margin to "50 basis points year-over-year" from 80. Delivered: Q2 2026 came in at 18.2% against 18.9%, a 70 basis-point decline — slightly worse than the 50 guided, but inside a fair band. **Delivered, marginally light.**
- **Germany.** Q1 2026 called it "clearly bottoming out" with automotive still declining. Q2 2026: Germany +4%, from −4%. **Delivered.**
- **Volume inflection.** Q4 2025 claimed a solid December exit rate and a flattish January, and predicted "supported revenue trends into Q1." Q1 2026 delivered +0.4% organic. **Delivered.**
- **The Netherlands labour legislation.** Q4 2025 refused to be drawn on the size of the effect and pushed back hard on an analyst's 15% bill-rate figure — "that's way, way too high" — guiding instead that higher bill rates would offset volume pressure. Q2 2026 outcome: the Netherlands down 1%, "finding its new equilibrium," with "some of the price increases having a dilutive effect on our gross margins." **Delivered, and the pushback was correct.**

The screener's earnings-beat record of 4 of 7 quarters (57%) understates this; on the operational commitments actually made on these calls, the hit rate is higher. There is no sandbagging pattern — if anything the opposite, since management repeatedly guided margin *down* into quarters where the revenue news was improving. That is the behaviour of a team managing expectations honestly rather than harvesting easy beats.

**The one deduction:** the persistent reliance on an adjusted profit measure running about 29% above statutory operating profit, and the promotion of the recovery ratio — a metric that flatters a business whose fee base is shrinking.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Four themes recur, and management's answers get thinner as you move down the list.

1. **Gross margin — asked on every single call, never resolved.** Simon LeChipre of Jefferies in February 2026 put the contradiction directly: "you are pointing to top line momentum improving into Q1 and particularly in North America, which should help gross margin. But your guidance suggests gross margin being down 90 bps year-on-year in Q1, which is a sequential deterioration." The answer was a request not to look at single quarters — "I tried to... break out a little bit from the fog and the mist of one quarter and the other." James Rowland Clark of Barclays asked the structural version in Q1 2026 — what would it actually take for the mix effect to ease — and got a bridge of basis points rather than an answer. **This is the unresolved question in the file, and it is the one that decides the investment case.**

2. **What the digital marketplace is actually worth.** Pressed twice. In February 2026 on why the revenue figure had not moved quarter on quarter, the answer was "it's just a matter of technicalities" and a refusal to set a target. In Q1 2026, asked directly for the profit benefit, the chief executive conceded: "it's hard to tell at this particular point in time... we want to start sketching the picture of the new asset, including the economics over the next couple of quarters." Two years into the flagship strategic initiative, its economics remain undisclosed. Productivity proxies are offered instead — fill rate up about 1%, employees per full-time-equivalent up 6% to 7%. Those are real, but they are inputs, not profit.

3. **Working capital as growth returns.** Maarten Verbeek of The Idea asked the right question in Q2 2026: staffing recoveries consume cash, 2025's cash flow was helped by working capital, and this year it may reverse. The answer conceded the mechanism — "obviously it does require investments in working capital" — then redirected to full-year framing and "last four quarters and running four quarters." No number was given. Free cash flow in the quarter had more than halved.

4. **Whether professional weakness is cyclical or structural.** Remi Grenu of Morgan Stanley asked explicitly in Q2 2025 whether there was anything "more structural versus the cyclicality." The chief executive's answer was entirely cyclical — companies defer discretionary hires when uncertain — and dismissed the structural reading. Professional has now declined for a further four quarters (−6% in Q2 2026) and permanent placement has been depressed for over three years. Analysts stopped asking. The question did not stop being valid.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Gross margin has fallen for four straight years and is still falling.** 20.86% (2022) → 18.67% (2025) → 18.2% (Q2 2026). Every call in this sequence guided it lower.

🔴 **Gross profit fell about 2% year-over-year in Q2 2026 even as revenue grew 1.9%.** The recovery is adding volume and subtracting spread. All of the quarter's profit growth came from costs.

🔴 **The profit growth lever is finite.** Operating costs are already €181m lower than 2024 and headcount has been cut for eight consecutive quarters. Q2 2026 captured seasonal demand "without adding any new capacity" — a claim that cannot be repeated indefinitely if growth accelerates.

🔴 **Free cash flow more than halved in Q2 2026** (€39m against €82m), and working capital turns into a headwind precisely as growth returns. Management confirmed the mechanism and declined to quantify it.

🔴 **The adjusted-to-statutory gap is large and permanent.** €720m against €512m for 2025; €182m against €145m in Q2 2026. The excluded items recur every year.

🔴 **Returns are below any reasonable cost of capital.** Return on invested capital of roughly 6% on a trailing basis, return on equity 8.2%. This is not currently a value-creating business.

🔴 **Insider buying is zero.** No management purchases through a period in which the shares fell to €21.30 and then rose 74%.

🟢 **The volume recovery is real, broad and verified.** From about 25% of the business growing at end-2024, to over 50% (Q4 2025), to 63% (Q1 2026), with Germany (+4%), the United Kingdom and France all crossing back into growth by Q2 2026 and United States operational growing for six consecutive quarters (+13% in Q2 2026).

🟢 **Management credibility is high.** Cost promises over-delivered, the German bottoming call was right, the Netherlands legislation call was right, and the pushback on an analyst's exaggerated bill-rate figure was correct.

🟢 **The balance sheet is sound.** Leverage of 1.8 times, net debt down €66m year-over-year, and a covenant profile that carries no visible near-term stress.

🟢 **Productivity gains are genuine and measurable.** Employees per full-time-equivalent up 6% to 7% year-over-year, over 50% of talent validation handled centrally, 1.7 million self-scheduled shifts in Q2 2026.

🟢 **Portfolio discipline.** Selling subscale technology and consulting units to LTM rather than defending a position where "we are a very small player" is the correct decision, honestly explained.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from price to volume.** Early in the sequence management spoke about protecting profitability. By Q2 2026 the language is fill rates, shifts, employees working, talent per full-time-equivalent — all volume and productivity measures. The chief executive appears aware of the risk and inserted a guard-rail in Q2 2026: "we are always very keen to have not only volume but also value... volume with no value is just spinning wheels." Naming the failure mode is not the same as avoiding it, and the gross margin says which way it is going.

**Who the customer now is.** The repeated, unprompted emphasis on large clients and on procurement is the most important disclosure in the file. In Q2 2025: "in many clients, large clients in the United States, we share from a procurement perspective as it relates to suppliers. If we have a better proposition... we can do well in terms of procurement rate." Randstad is winning share by being the fastest and cheapest supplier into professional procurement departments. That is a genuine operational advantage — and it is precisely the customer set with the most bargaining power and the least willingness to leave a spread on the table. The productivity gains are being handed to clients, not retained.

**The artificial-intelligence defence is a positioning statement.** The Q1 2026 remarks split the business into an artificial-intelligence-resistant two-thirds (operational, health care: welders, technicians, nurses) and, by silence, a threatened remainder. The threatened remainder — professional, permanent placement, digital, recruitment process outsourcing — is the high-spread third, and it has been shrinking throughout the entire sequence. Management's own framing concedes that the durable part of the business is the low-margin part.

**Management is automating its own fee away.** The Torc platform is presented as an achievement in these words: "resulting in 50% lower recruiting cost and 50% shorter time to fill" (Q2 2026). In a competitive market, a 50% reduction in the cost of performing a service ends up in the client's pocket. This is the mechanism behind the four-year spread compression, described from the seller's side as a triumph.

**New voices.** A chief digital growth officer arrived from Booking.com in February 2026 — a consumer-platform hire, not a staffing hire, and a clear statement of where management believes the terminal business model lies. It is also an implicit admission that the existing organisation could not build it.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.** The operating trajectory has genuinely inflected. Revenue is growing again after eleven quarters of decline, the growth is broad rather than concentrated, costs are permanently lower, productivity is measurably better, the balance sheet is sound, and management has been consistently truthful. On the business, the direction of travel is not in doubt.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Separate the *volume* recovery from the *earnings* recovery, because only the first one has arrived. Randstad earns a spread on billed hours, and that spread has compressed for four consecutive years — including in the quarter that produced the recovery headline, where gross profit fell about 2% while revenue grew 1.9%. Every euro of the Q2 2026 profit improvement came from cost reduction, a lever that is eight quarters old and finite. The director must decide whether the spread compression is cyclical mix — depressed permanent and professional placement, which recovers late in every cycle — or structural, driven by a shift toward large procurement-led clients and by Randstad's own automation lowering the cost of the service it sells. Management's answers on this point have been the least satisfying in the entire file, and it is the only question that determines whether normalized earnings are near €3.30 a share or near €2.10.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is scale and local density — Randstad is the largest staffing firm in the world, with route density in its core markets and, increasingly, a genuine technology advantage in fill rates and time-to-fill. That advantage is real, but the returns evidence says it is not being retained: gross margin down four straight years, operating margin before amortization down from about 4.4% at the 2022 peak to 3.1%, return on invested capital of roughly 6% and return on equity of 8.2% — below any plausible cost of capital. Under the standard used here, a falling return-and-margin profile is an eroding moat regardless of the scale position behind it. The most telling evidence is that the firm's clearest source of competitive advantage — the digital marketplace — is showing up in market share and fill rates but not in the spread.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is the deflation of labour-arbitrage economics: a business that bills hours at a spread while automation decouples revenue from headcount and erodes bill-rate power. Two-thirds of Randstad — operational and health care — is genuinely defensible; nobody automates a welder or a care worker this decade, and the employment-liability, compliance and supply functions Randstad performs are not what artificial intelligence replaces. But the high-spread third is squarely exposed, it has been shrinking for three years, and the firm is itself demonstrating that the cost of matching a candidate to a job can fall by half. That impairs the mix, not the existence, of the business.

**Cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a clean value trap, and at today's price mostly spent.** When these shares traded at €21.30 the market was pricing terminal decline into a solvent, cash-generative global leader, and that was a mispricing. At €37.05 — up about 74% from that low and roughly 29% above the 200-day average — the trailing multiple is about 21 times earnings and 9.8 times enterprise value to reported cash profits, a premium to both Adecco and ManpowerGroup on live, post-rally multiples. The fear-print has been harvested. What remains is a fairly-priced cyclical with an eroding spread, which is a different proposition entirely.

It also sits badly against oil near USD 89 with the Hormuz blockade reinstated, a proposed replacement tariff regime that lands on European exporters, and a December rate rise as the priced base case, which means no help from falling rates. Positioning is full, and in this tape negative surprises travel farther than positive ones.

What would change the call. The business deserves to stay on the list: management is credible and has delivered what it promised, the balance sheet is sound at 1.8 times leverage, shareholders are paid about 4.4%, and the operating direction is genuinely improving. The level to wait for is roughly EUR 29 to EUR 30 - back toward the 200-day average of EUR 28.70 - where the parts-based work implies a real double-digit discount instead of a small premium and the free-cash-flow yield becomes compelling again. The alternative route in, without waiting for that price, is to require the proof: two or three consecutive quarters in which gross profit grows faster than revenue, converting the volume story into an earnings story. Neither condition is met today, so the position is a watch, not a buy.
