# Forensic Dossier — Randstad N.V. (RAND.AS)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Listing:** Euronext Amsterdam, quoted in euros · **Price used:** €37.05 (live quote, 2026-07-27)
**Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 (Apr 23, 2025) · Q2 2025 (Jul 23, 2025) · Q4/FY 2025 (Feb 11, 2026) · Q1 2026 (Apr 22, 2026) · Q2 2026 (Jul 22, 2026)

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story travels a clean arc from *survival* to *vindication* — and management deserves credit for how little the story wobbled on the way.

**Early 2025 — protect the floor.** The opening posture was defensive and honest about it. Chief executive Sander van 't Noordende opened Q1 2025 with "we were able to protect our bottom line," and the operative verbs were protect, adapt, steer. The chief financial officer, Jorge Vazquez, framed the entire quarter as cost discipline: "our gross profit and OpEx were aligned allowing us to protect relative profitability despite the lower top line." Revenue was falling 4.2% and the honest admission was that visibility had gone: "macroeconomic uncertainty has gone up, which is limiting visibility."

**Mid 2025 — the new normal.** By Q2 2025 uncertainty had been reframed from a shock into a permanent condition — "which, frankly, we and many of our clients see as the new normal." The emphasis shifted from cost defence toward the strategic build: specialization, digital marketplaces, the "partner for talent" programme. This is where the *transformation* narrative started carrying weight the financials could not yet carry.

**Early 2026 — the turn is claimed.** The Q4 2025 call (February 2026) is the hinge. Management produced its first genuinely forward-leaning claim in two years: "we now have over 50% of the business in growth compared to around 25% at the end of 2024," a December exit rate described as solid, and a January trend described as flattish. A new chief digital growth officer was hired from Booking.com — a signal about where the story was heading.

**Mid 2026 — vindication, and a pre-emptive defence.** Q1 2026 delivered the return to organic growth (+0.4%, with 63% of the business growing), and Q2 2026 broadened it (+1.9%, with Germany and the United Kingdom back to growth). But the most revealing passage of the whole sequence is unprompted: in Q1 2026 the chief executive volunteered a long, structured defence of the business against artificial intelligence — citing studies pointing to "a job loss of 6% to 7% over the next 5 to 10 years," and arguing that "Randstad operational and health care are 2/3 of our business today. These are typically jobs that are human-centric and minimally impacted by AI." Management does not spend four minutes of prepared remarks pre-empting a question unless it knows that question is the one holding the shares down.

**Quietly dropped:** the digital marketplace revenue milestone. It was introduced with fanfare (about €4 billion annualized), then stalled — an analyst caught it in February 2026: "In the third quarter, you mentioned that your digital marketplace generated EUR 4 billion in annualized revenue, and exactly the same you mentioned today. So why haven't we seen any progress quarter-on-quarter?" The metric has since been replaced in the script by shift counts, which grow faster and mean less.

**Quietly added:** portfolio pruning. In Q2 2026 the technology and consulting units in Australia, France, Germany, Belgium and Luxembourg were put up for sale to LTM — a business the chief executive characterised as one where "we are a very small player."

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where the story and the numbers part company. The claims about *volume* are true. The claims about *earning power* are considerably richer than the trajectory justifies.

| Management claim | Where | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our overall revenue growth is picking up, delivering 1.9% organic growth" | Q2 2026 | Revenue €5,897m, organic +1.9%, against a consensus of about 1.0%. Real, and a genuine beat. | **Holds** |
| "Profitability is also up year-over-year" | Q2 2026 | Underlying operating profit before amortization of €182m vs €171m, +6%. True for the quarter. | **Holds, narrowly** |
| Implied: the recovery is improving the economics | Throughout | Gross margin fell to 18.2% from 18.9% a year earlier. Gross profit — the fee Randstad actually keeps — was roughly €1,073m against about €1,096m, i.e. **down about 2% while revenue grew 1.9%.** | **Diverges — materially** |
| "The scalability we've built into our operating model... is starting to show financial gearing" | Q2 2026 | All €11m of the profit improvement came from operating costs, not from gross profit, which shrank. This is cost gearing on a shrinking fee base, not operating leverage on a growing one. | **Poorer than told** |
| "Our recovery ratio of over 80% over the last 4 quarters" | Q2 2026 | Recovery ratio measures profit retained against gross profit *lost*. Management defined it themselves in Q4 2025: "we've been able to expand EBITDA year-over-year more than the gross profit we lost." Quoting a decline-era metric approvingly in a growth quarter is a tell. | **Misleading framing** |
| "Solid free cash flow of approximately EUR 600 million" for 2025 | Q4 2025 | True for 2025. But Q2 2026 free cash flow was €39m against €82m a year earlier — less than half — on working capital and tax. The 2025 figure was flattered by a working-capital release the chief financial officer himself flagged as non-repeating: "there is a spillover effect from the very strong 2025." | **Holds for 2025, decaying now** |
| "EUR 181 million lower cost in 2025 than in 2024" | Q4 2025 | Corroborated: total operating expenses fell from €4,296m (2024) to €3,797m (2025). Delivered, and then some. | **Holds** |
| Five-year franchise health (implied by the transformation story) | Throughout | Gross profit: €5,751m (2022) → €5,278m (2023) → €4,701m (2024) → **€4,309m (2025)**. Gross margin: 20.86% → 20.76% → 19.49% → **18.67%**, and 18.2% in the latest quarter. Return on invested capital is about 6% on a trailing basis. | **Diverges — this is a four-year, unbroken compression** |

**The single most important forensic finding.** Randstad is a spread business: it bills a worker's hours to a client and keeps the difference. That difference is the gross margin, and it has fallen every year for four years — from 20.86% in 2022 to 18.2% in the most recent quarter, a loss of more than a quarter of the spread. The recovery now under way is being won in the *lowest*-spread part of the business, from the *most* powerful buyers. Management says so plainly: growth is "largely led by increasing demand in large clients" (Q2 2026), and in Q2 2025 the chief financial officer conceded the mechanism outright — "these larger clients... they are growing high single digits. That has an impact in our margin."

**A second finding on the headline profit number.** The €182m of quarterly profit everyone quotes is an adjusted figure. Statutory operating profit in the same quarter was €145m, and net income €84m. For the 2025 full year the same gap runs €720m adjusted against €512m statutory — roughly €208m of amortization and "one-off" costs excluded. Those one-offs have appeared every single year of this sequence. A cost that recurs annually is not a one-off, and a multiple built on the adjusted number overstates what the business earns by close to 30%.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — genuinely, and earned.** This is the strongest dimension in the file.

- **Q1 2025 — defensive, hedged.** "It's too early to say with any certainty what impact this will have on our markets and on our future performance." On protecting margin: "It's impossible to guarantee, but that's how we're looking at the year."
- **Q2 2025 — steady, strategy-forward.** "All in all, we're absolutely on the right track." The confidence is about the plan, not the numbers.
- **Q4 2025 — the first forward commitment.** "We couldn't be better positioned for a more complete recovery." And on 2026: "I'm pretty sure we've built the ability to improve the results and profitability going forward" — the first unhedged forward statement in the sequence.
- **Q1 2026 — confident, and confident enough to take on the bear case.** "The current trajectory of our business gives us confidence for the months ahead," plus the unprompted artificial-intelligence defence.
- **Q2 2026 — assured.** "This gives me confidence in our ability to show progress for the rest of the year in both revenue and profit growth."

The language migrated from defensive (protect, adapt, steer, adaptability) to offensive (capture, gearing, scalability, accelerate). Importantly, the specificity moved in the same direction: by Q1 2026 the chief financial officer was giving quarter-ahead gross-margin bridges to ten basis points. Executives who are worried get vaguer, not more precise. This one got more precise.

The one asymmetry worth flagging: confidence rose fastest on *revenue* and stayed carefully hedged on *margin*. Every single call in this sequence guided gross margin down. That is not a company that believes its spread is about to recover.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is a management team that says what will happen and is then largely right — including when the news is bad.

Tracked promises against later delivery:

- **Cost.** Q1 2025 promised roughly €60m of year-over-year savings entering the year with "headroom into the next quarters." The 2025 outturn was €181m lower costs and a 71% recovery ratio. **Over-delivered.**
- **Gross margin.** Q2 2025 guided a Q3 seasonal dip of "around 20 to 30 basis points" plus a foreign-exchange drag. Q1 2026 guided the Q2 temp margin to "50 basis points year-over-year" from 80. Delivered: Q2 2026 came in at 18.2% against 18.9%, a 70 basis-point decline — slightly worse than the 50 guided, but inside a fair band. **Delivered, marginally light.**
- **Germany.** Q1 2026 called it "clearly bottoming out" with automotive still declining. Q2 2026: Germany +4%, from −4%. **Delivered.**
- **Volume inflection.** Q4 2025 claimed a solid December exit rate and a flattish January, and predicted "supported revenue trends into Q1." Q1 2026 delivered +0.4% organic. **Delivered.**
- **The Netherlands labour legislation.** Q4 2025 refused to be drawn on the size of the effect and pushed back hard on an analyst's 15% bill-rate figure — "that's way, way too high" — guiding instead that higher bill rates would offset volume pressure. Q2 2026 outcome: the Netherlands down 1%, "finding its new equilibrium," with "some of the price increases having a dilutive effect on our gross margins." **Delivered, and the pushback was correct.**

The screener's earnings-beat record of 4 of 7 quarters (57%) understates this; on the operational commitments actually made on these calls, the hit rate is higher. There is no sandbagging pattern — if anything the opposite, since management repeatedly guided margin *down* into quarters where the revenue news was improving. That is the behaviour of a team managing expectations honestly rather than harvesting easy beats.

**The one deduction:** the persistent reliance on an adjusted profit measure running about 29% above statutory operating profit, and the promotion of the recovery ratio — a metric that flatters a business whose fee base is shrinking.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Four themes recur, and management's answers get thinner as you move down the list.

1. **Gross margin — asked on every single call, never resolved.** Simon LeChipre of Jefferies in February 2026 put the contradiction directly: "you are pointing to top line momentum improving into Q1 and particularly in North America, which should help gross margin. But your guidance suggests gross margin being down 90 bps year-on-year in Q1, which is a sequential deterioration." The answer was a request not to look at single quarters — "I tried to... break out a little bit from the fog and the mist of one quarter and the other." James Rowland Clark of Barclays asked the structural version in Q1 2026 — what would it actually take for the mix effect to ease — and got a bridge of basis points rather than an answer. **This is the unresolved question in the file, and it is the one that decides the investment case.**

2. **What the digital marketplace is actually worth.** Pressed twice. In February 2026 on why the revenue figure had not moved quarter on quarter, the answer was "it's just a matter of technicalities" and a refusal to set a target. In Q1 2026, asked directly for the profit benefit, the chief executive conceded: "it's hard to tell at this particular point in time... we want to start sketching the picture of the new asset, including the economics over the next couple of quarters." Two years into the flagship strategic initiative, its economics remain undisclosed. Productivity proxies are offered instead — fill rate up about 1%, employees per full-time-equivalent up 6% to 7%. Those are real, but they are inputs, not profit.

3. **Working capital as growth returns.** Maarten Verbeek of The Idea asked the right question in Q2 2026: staffing recoveries consume cash, 2025's cash flow was helped by working capital, and this year it may reverse. The answer conceded the mechanism — "obviously it does require investments in working capital" — then redirected to full-year framing and "last four quarters and running four quarters." No number was given. Free cash flow in the quarter had more than halved.

4. **Whether professional weakness is cyclical or structural.** Remi Grenu of Morgan Stanley asked explicitly in Q2 2025 whether there was anything "more structural versus the cyclicality." The chief executive's answer was entirely cyclical — companies defer discretionary hires when uncertain — and dismissed the structural reading. Professional has now declined for a further four quarters (−6% in Q2 2026) and permanent placement has been depressed for over three years. Analysts stopped asking. The question did not stop being valid.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Gross margin has fallen for four straight years and is still falling.** 20.86% (2022) → 18.67% (2025) → 18.2% (Q2 2026). Every call in this sequence guided it lower.

🔴 **Gross profit fell about 2% year-over-year in Q2 2026 even as revenue grew 1.9%.** The recovery is adding volume and subtracting spread. All of the quarter's profit growth came from costs.

🔴 **The profit growth lever is finite.** Operating costs are already €181m lower than 2024 and headcount has been cut for eight consecutive quarters. Q2 2026 captured seasonal demand "without adding any new capacity" — a claim that cannot be repeated indefinitely if growth accelerates.

🔴 **Free cash flow more than halved in Q2 2026** (€39m against €82m), and working capital turns into a headwind precisely as growth returns. Management confirmed the mechanism and declined to quantify it.

🔴 **The adjusted-to-statutory gap is large and permanent.** €720m against €512m for 2025; €182m against €145m in Q2 2026. The excluded items recur every year.

🔴 **Returns are below any reasonable cost of capital.** Return on invested capital of roughly 6% on a trailing basis, return on equity 8.2%. This is not currently a value-creating business.

🔴 **Insider buying is zero.** No management purchases through a period in which the shares fell to €21.30 and then rose 74%.

🟢 **The volume recovery is real, broad and verified.** From about 25% of the business growing at end-2024, to over 50% (Q4 2025), to 63% (Q1 2026), with Germany (+4%), the United Kingdom and France all crossing back into growth by Q2 2026 and United States operational growing for six consecutive quarters (+13% in Q2 2026).

🟢 **Management credibility is high.** Cost promises over-delivered, the German bottoming call was right, the Netherlands legislation call was right, and the pushback on an analyst's exaggerated bill-rate figure was correct.

🟢 **The balance sheet is sound.** Leverage of 1.8 times, net debt down €66m year-over-year, and a covenant profile that carries no visible near-term stress.

🟢 **Productivity gains are genuine and measurable.** Employees per full-time-equivalent up 6% to 7% year-over-year, over 50% of talent validation handled centrally, 1.7 million self-scheduled shifts in Q2 2026.

🟢 **Portfolio discipline.** Selling subscale technology and consulting units to LTM rather than defending a position where "we are a very small player" is the correct decision, honestly explained.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary migrated from price to volume.** Early in the sequence management spoke about protecting profitability. By Q2 2026 the language is fill rates, shifts, employees working, talent per full-time-equivalent — all volume and productivity measures. The chief executive appears aware of the risk and inserted a guard-rail in Q2 2026: "we are always very keen to have not only volume but also value... volume with no value is just spinning wheels." Naming the failure mode is not the same as avoiding it, and the gross margin says which way it is going.

**Who the customer now is.** The repeated, unprompted emphasis on large clients and on procurement is the most important disclosure in the file. In Q2 2025: "in many clients, large clients in the United States, we share from a procurement perspective as it relates to suppliers. If we have a better proposition... we can do well in terms of procurement rate." Randstad is winning share by being the fastest and cheapest supplier into professional procurement departments. That is a genuine operational advantage — and it is precisely the customer set with the most bargaining power and the least willingness to leave a spread on the table. The productivity gains are being handed to clients, not retained.

**The artificial-intelligence defence is a positioning statement.** The Q1 2026 remarks split the business into an artificial-intelligence-resistant two-thirds (operational, health care: welders, technicians, nurses) and, by silence, a threatened remainder. The threatened remainder — professional, permanent placement, digital, recruitment process outsourcing — is the high-spread third, and it has been shrinking throughout the entire sequence. Management's own framing concedes that the durable part of the business is the low-margin part.

**Management is automating its own fee away.** The Torc platform is presented as an achievement in these words: "resulting in 50% lower recruiting cost and 50% shorter time to fill" (Q2 2026). In a competitive market, a 50% reduction in the cost of performing a service ends up in the client's pocket. This is the mechanism behind the four-year spread compression, described from the seller's side as a triumph.

**New voices.** A chief digital growth officer arrived from Booking.com in February 2026 — a consumer-platform hire, not a staffing hire, and a clear statement of where management believes the terminal business model lies. It is also an implicit admission that the existing organisation could not build it.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.** The operating trajectory has genuinely inflected. Revenue is growing again after eleven quarters of decline, the growth is broad rather than concentrated, costs are permanently lower, productivity is measurably better, the balance sheet is sound, and management has been consistently truthful. On the business, the direction of travel is not in doubt.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Separate the *volume* recovery from the *earnings* recovery, because only the first one has arrived. Randstad earns a spread on billed hours, and that spread has compressed for four consecutive years — including in the quarter that produced the recovery headline, where gross profit fell about 2% while revenue grew 1.9%. Every euro of the Q2 2026 profit improvement came from cost reduction, a lever that is eight quarters old and finite. The director must decide whether the spread compression is cyclical mix — depressed permanent and professional placement, which recovers late in every cycle — or structural, driven by a shift toward large procurement-led clients and by Randstad's own automation lowering the cost of the service it sells. Management's answers on this point have been the least satisfying in the entire file, and it is the only question that determines whether normalized earnings are near €3.30 a share or near €2.10.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is scale and local density — Randstad is the largest staffing firm in the world, with route density in its core markets and, increasingly, a genuine technology advantage in fill rates and time-to-fill. That advantage is real, but the returns evidence says it is not being retained: gross margin down four straight years, operating margin before amortization down from about 4.4% at the 2022 peak to 3.1%, return on invested capital of roughly 6% and return on equity of 8.2% — below any plausible cost of capital. Under the standard used here, a falling return-and-margin profile is an eroding moat regardless of the scale position behind it. The most telling evidence is that the firm's clearest source of competitive advantage — the digital marketplace — is showing up in market share and fill rates but not in the spread.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is the deflation of labour-arbitrage economics: a business that bills hours at a spread while automation decouples revenue from headcount and erodes bill-rate power. Two-thirds of Randstad — operational and health care — is genuinely defensible; nobody automates a welder or a care worker this decade, and the employment-liability, compliance and supply functions Randstad performs are not what artificial intelligence replaces. But the high-spread third is squarely exposed, it has been shrinking for three years, and the firm is itself demonstrating that the cost of matching a candidate to a job can fall by half. That impairs the mix, not the existence, of the business.

**Cheapness: neither a clean fear-print nor a clean value trap, and at today's price mostly spent.** When these shares traded at €21.30 the market was pricing terminal decline into a solvent, cash-generative global leader, and that was a mispricing. At €37.05 — up about 74% from that low and roughly 29% above the 200-day average — the trailing multiple is about 21 times earnings and 9.8 times enterprise value to reported cash profits, a premium to both Adecco and ManpowerGroup on live, post-rally multiples. The fear-print has been harvested. What remains is a fairly-priced cyclical with an eroding spread, which is a different proposition entirely.
